authoring.value:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x)$ whose ordinary integral exists over the interval, the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

Notice that $f(x) =  x\cos x$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x) =  x\cos x$ is an odd function, we have

$$
\int_{-1}^{1} x\cos x  \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+A & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$

The displayed example integrands are continuous on their intervals. If an integrand has an internal singularity, first check the convergence of every one-sided improper integral; symmetry cannot cancel independently divergent integrals. A Cauchy principal value requires an explicit principal-value convention.
authoring.rationale: The actual example integrands are continuous, but the universal symmetry rule must require existence of the ordinary integral. Qualify the rule and explicitly distinguish ordinary improper convergence from principal-value regularization. Original source prompt, answer fields, and historical original solution remain preserved.
